s: A level of abstraction in the architecture stack (business, conceptual, semantic, information, logical, physical, technical) with its own questions, artifacts and decision rights.
x: Architecture Layer Definition An Architecture Layer is a level of abstraction in the architecture stack with its own questions, artifacts and decision rights. This knowledge base distinguishes seven layers (machine-readable in 00-system/taxonomy/layers.yaml ): Layer Central question Typical decisions --- --- --- --- 1 Business What does the organisation do and need? scope, business rules, accountability 2 Conceptual Which things and relationships matter? concept scope, high-level relationships 3 Semantic What exactly does each concept mean? definitions, identity, specialization, equivalence 4 Information How is meaning represented as information structures, paradigm-independent? classes, attributes, cardinalities, information-level history 5 Logical Data How is information structured in a chosen paradigm? normalization, keys, temporal modeling approach 6 Physical Data How is the logical model realized in a store? data types, partitioning, indexing, physical history mechanism 7 Technical Implementation Which technologies and operations implement it? products, pipelines, deployment Explanation Layers are not interchangeable . A decision taken at the wrong layer produces lock-in or ambiguity: e.g. defining the meaning of "customer" in a physical table comment (Implicit Semantics) or choosing a history mechanism before stating the historical requirement (Historical Requirements Are Explicit). s: The ability to take, record, govern and trace architecture decisions consistently across teams.
x: Architecture Decision Management Capability Description Taking decisions with explicit criteria and options, recording them, approving them with the right decision rights, and tracing them to implementation. Outcomes Fewer re-debated decisions; auditable architecture; faster onboarding. Enablers Architecture Decision Framework, Decision Rights Model, decision trees and scoring models. Maturity Indicators Level Indicator --- --- 1 Fragmented Decisions in meeting notes and e-mail 2 Documented ADRs written for some decisions 3 Structured ADRs linked to principles, patterns and architectures 4 Governed Approval per decision rights, recorded and auditable 5 Executable Decision logic and rules executed by tools; decisions validated against implementations

s: The ability of an organisation to reconstruct past states of its data - as they were true and as they were known - for operations, audit and regulation.
x: Historical Data Reconstruction Capability Description Reconstructing past states on demand, with the time dimensions the business actually requires. Outcomes Reproducible reports and decisions; defensible audits; correct handling of backdated corrections. Enablers Historical Requirements Are Explicit, Database History Pattern Decision Tree, history patterns, platform support such as SQL Server Temporal Tables. Maturity Indicators Level Indicator --- --- 1 Fragmented History reconstructed ad hoc from backups and logs 2 Documented History requirements described per system 3 Structured History requirements in information models; patterns chosen with the decision tree 4 Governed History decisions recorded and approved; retention governed 5 Executable History requirements validated automatically against physical models

s: A justified choice between alternatives that affects the structure, qualities or constraints of an architecture, recorded independently of the architecture documentation it shapes.
x: Architecture Decision Definition An Architecture Decision is a justified choice between alternatives that affects the structure, qualities or constraints of an architecture. It is recorded as a separate object (an Architecture Decision Record, ADR) so it can be traced, reviewed and superseded independently of the documentation it shapes. Explanation A decision record captures: context, problem, options, evaluation criteria, trade-offs, decision, consequences, assumptions and constraints. Recording decisions separately supports traceability from knowledge to implementation. Decisions belong to a layer: semantic decisions (meaning) are taken by different roles than physical design decisions (see Decision Rights Model). In this knowledge base, reusable decisions are captured as decision records (e.g. Select Historical Data Strategy) and their logic as decision trees (e.g. Database History Pattern Decision Tree). Distinctions - A decision is not a principle : a principle guides many decisions; a decision applies in a context. - A decision tree encodes reusable decision logic; a decision record documents one decision (or one reusable decision archetype). - A governance decision (approval/rejection of an artifact by a governance body) is a different object type ( governance-decision ). Examples - "Use a bitemporal model for policy data because retroactive corrections must be reconstructable." - Use Markdown and Git as the Initial Knowledge Store.

s: The discipline and resulting structures that define how an organisation's data is described, organised, integrated, governed and realized across systems, from business meaning to technical implementation.
x: Data Architecture Definition Data Architecture is the discipline and the resulting set of structures that define how an organisation's data is described, organised, integrated, governed and realized across systems — from business meaning down to technical implementation. Explanation Data Architecture spans the whole Architecture Layer stack. It is not a single model or a single platform; it is the coherent set of decisions that determine: - which data exists and what it means (in cooperation with semantic and information architecture); - how data is structured (data models at conceptual, logical and physical level); - where data is authoritative and how it moves (Data Integration, Each Data Element Has an Authoritative Source); - how data is stored and processed (Data Platform); - how data changes over time (Data Lifecycle, Temporal Data Management); - how all of this is governed (Data Governance, Architecture Governance Model). Its outputs are models, principles, standards, patterns, architecture decisions and reference architectures. Distinctions - Not the same as Information Architecture : information architecture focuses on the structure and meaning of information as used by people and processes; data architecture additionally covers realization, integration, platforms and operations. The boundary is contested (see Open Questions). - Not the same as a Data Platform : a platform is one realization component of the architecture. - Not the same as data modeling (Data Model):

s: The structuring of information — its meaning, organisation, classification and relationships — so that people and processes can find, understand and use it consistently.
x: Information Architecture Definition Information Architecture is the structuring of information — its meaning, organisation, classification and relationships — so that people and processes can find, understand and use it consistently. Explanation Information architecture concentrates on the upper and middle layers: which information the organisation needs, how it is classified (Taxonomy), how it is represented as an Information Model, and how it relates to business processes. It consumes meaning from the Semantic Model and hands representation choices to the Logical Data Model. Distinctions - Compared with Data Architecture: information architecture is more concerned with meaning, structure and use; data architecture additionally addresses realization, integration, storage and operations. - In user-experience design, "information architecture" also denotes navigation and content structure of websites. That usage is out of scope here. Examples - A classification scheme for product documents used by several departments. - An information model of "Case", "Party" and "Decision" for a public-sector organisation. Open Questions - Different frameworks draw the boundary with data architecture differently; flagged, not resolved.

s: Derive models layer by layer - governed concepts, then information model, then logical, then physical - keeping a traceability link at every step.
x: Layered Model Derivation Purpose A repeatable way to go from business meaning to implementation without taking decisions at the wrong layer. Steps 1. Identify and govern the business concepts in scope (semantic layer). 2. Represent them in an Information Model, stating history and quality requirements. 3. Realize the information model in a Logical Data Model for the chosen paradigm; record paradigm and history decisions as ADRs. 4. Realize the logical model in a Physical Data Model for the chosen store. 5. At each step, link every element to the element it realizes (Concept-to-Model Traceability) and run model validation (Model Validation Control). Inputs Governed concepts, requirements, principles, platform constraints. Outputs Information, logical and physical models with traceability links; ADRs per layer. When to Use Shared, governed or regulated data. For throw-away prototypes, steps may be compressed but concepts are backfilled.

s: Each architecture decision is taken at the layer where it belongs, by the role with decision rights for that layer, and lower layers do not silently override higher-layer decisions.
x: Decisions Belong to Their Layer Statement Each architecture decision shall be taken at the layer where it belongs, by the role with decision rights for that layer; lower layers shall not silently override decisions of higher layers. Rationale Mixing layers produces technology lock-in of meaning (e.g. semantics defined by a database product) and untraceable decisions. Implications - Decision records state their layer ( layer metadata). - A physical design that cannot honour an information-level requirement is escalated, not worked around (Architecture Change Process). Consequences - Positive: clean traceability, replaceable technology. - Negative: more explicit hand-offs between roles. Applicability All architecture work covered by this knowledge base. Exceptions Small solutions where one person holds all roles still record the layer, but may combine approval steps. Related Principles - Technology-Neutral Architecture First - Meaning Before Representation

t: Each Data Element Has an Authoritative Source
s: For every shared data element, exactly one authoritative source is designated; other copies are derived and traceable to it.
x: Each Data Element Has an Authoritative Source Statement For every shared data element, exactly one authoritative source shall be designated; other copies are derived and traceable to it. Rationale Multiple uncoordinated sources of the same fact produce contradictory answers and unresolvable reconciliation disputes. Implications - Authoritative source is recorded as metadata per data element or data set. - Copies are read-only derivations with lineage. - Where several systems legitimately create the same entity, a Master Data Hub defines authority per attribute. Consequences - Positive: defensible answers, simpler integration. - Negative: may require re-platforming data entry. Applicability Shared master, reference and key transactional data. Exceptions Transitional states during Data Migration, explicitly time-boxed. Related Principles - Data Has an Accountable Owner

s: Architecture is expressed in technology-neutral concepts and patterns first; technology-specific choices reference and realize them.
x: Technology-Neutral Architecture First Statement Architecture shall be expressed in technology-neutral concepts and patterns first; technology-specific choices shall reference and realize them. Rationale Technologies change faster than business meaning and architectural intent. Neutral architecture survives product replacement and allows fair comparison of alternatives. Implications - Every technology object links to the generic concept or pattern it implements. - Requirements are stated as capabilities before product selection. Consequences - Positive: portability, clearer evaluation of products. - Negative: an extra abstraction step; risk of "neutral" designs that ignore real platform constraints. Applicability Conceptual through logical layers; platform capability models. Exceptions When a technology is a hard constraint (e.g. mandated by enterprise standard), record it as a constraint in the relevant Architecture Decision. Related Principles - Decisions Belong to Their Layer

s: A structured representation of data — its entities, attributes, relationships and constraints — at a stated level of abstraction and for a stated purpose.
x: Data Model Definition A Data Model is a structured representation of data — its entities, attributes, relationships and constraints — at a stated level of abstraction and for a stated purpose. Explanation "Data model" is an umbrella term. A model is only meaningful when its level is explicit. This knowledge base distinguishes four model levels, each belonging to an Architecture Layer: Model Layer Answers --- --- --- Conceptual Data Model Conceptual Which things matter and how they relate? Information Model Information How is meaning represented, paradigm-independent? Logical Data Model Logical How is it structured in a paradigm (relational, dimensional, graph)? Physical Data Model Physical How is it realized in a specific store? Meaning itself is defined in the Semantic Model, not in the data model (Meaning Before Representation). Distinctions - A data model is not a database schema; a schema is one realization of a physical model. - A data model is not a Semantic Model: data models represent meaning, semantic models define it. Examples - An ER diagram of Party, Agreement and Product (conceptual). - A star schema with a Sales fact and Customer dimension (logical, dimensional paradigm).

s: A paradigm-independent model that represents governed meaning as information structures — classes, attributes, relationships, cardinalities and information-level constraints including history requirements.
x: Information Model Definition An Information Model represents governed meaning as information structures — classes, attributes, relationships, cardinalities and information-level constraints (including history requirements) — independent of any data paradigm or technology. Explanation The information model answers: how is the meaning defined in the Semantic Model represented in an information model? It is typically expressed in UML class diagrams or an equivalent notation. It is the layer at which information-level history requirements (valid time, transaction time) are stated, before a technical mechanism is chosen. Distinctions - Versus Semantic Model: the semantic model defines meaning (e.g. "a Customer is a Party with an active Agreement"); the information model represents it ("Customer: attribute customerSince 1..1"). - Versus Logical Data Model: the information model is paradigm-independent; the logical model commits to relational, dimensional, graph or document structures. - Some frameworks use "information model" and "logical data model" as synonyms. This knowledge base does not — flagged as interpretation. Examples - A UML class model of Party, Role, Agreement with multiplicities and a note "Agreement must be reconstructable as known at any past date". Open Questions - Needs validation whether the separation from the logical data model is useful for all target audiences.

s: The capture, storage and querying of how data and knowledge about data change over time, including valid time (when a fact is true in reality) and transaction time (when the fact was recorded).
x: Temporal Data Management Definition Temporal Data Management is the capture, storage and querying of how data — and knowledge about data — changes over time. Explanation Two time dimensions are commonly distinguished: - Valid time (application time, business time): when a fact is true in the modeled reality. - Transaction time (system time): when the fact was recorded in, and removed from, the database. A model supporting both is bitemporal . The concept is technology-neutral; it is realized by patterns such as Bitemporal Data Model, System-Versioned History Table, Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2 and Event Sourcing, and implemented by technologies such as SQL Server Temporal Tables. The requirement must be stated before the mechanism is chosen (Historical Requirements Are Explicit). The choice is supported by Database History Pattern Decision Tree. Distinctions - History versus audit : an audit trail records who changed what and when for accountability; history supports reconstruction and temporal querying. They overlap but are not identical. - History versus backup : backups restore a whole state; they are not a queryable history. Examples - "What was the customer's address on 1 March, as we knew it on 15 March?" requires both valid and transaction time.

s: A data model that identifies the business things of interest and their high-level relationships, without attributes' technical detail and independent of any implementation.
x: Conceptual Data Model Definition A Conceptual Data Model identifies the business things of interest and their high-level relationships, without technical detail and independent of any implementation. Explanation It fixes scope and vocabulary : which business concepts are in view and how they relate. It is the first data model to be agreed with business stakeholders and a key input to the Information Model. Every entity should trace to a governed concept (Concept-to-Model Traceability). Distinctions - Versus Semantic Model: a conceptual model shows which concepts and relationships matter; the semantic model states precisely what they mean (definitions, identity criteria, specialization, equivalence). In many practices these are merged; this knowledge base keeps them separate (see Architecture Layer). - Versus Logical Data Model: no keys, no normalization, no paradigm. Examples - "A Customer holds one or more Agreements; an Agreement covers one or more Products."

s: A data model that structures information in a chosen data paradigm (e.g. relational, dimensional, graph, document) with keys, relationships and constraints, independent of a specific product.
x: Logical Data Model Definition A Logical Data Model structures information in a chosen data paradigm — relational, dimensional, graph, document — with keys, relationships and constraints, independent of a specific database product. Explanation Decisions at this layer include normalization level, identifier strategy, the temporal modeling approach (e.g. Bitemporal Data Model versus Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2) and paradigm-specific structures. It realizes the information model and is realized by the Physical Data Model. Distinctions - Not product-specific: data types are logical (e.g. "date", "amount"), not DATETIME2(7) . - Not paradigm-independent: that is the Information Model. Examples - A third-normal-form relational model of orders with surrogate and natural keys. - A dimensional model with a Sales fact and conformed Customer dimension.

s: A data model that specifies how a logical data model is realized in a specific data store, including data types, storage structures, indexing, partitioning and physical history mechanisms.
x: Physical Data Model Definition A Physical Data Model specifies how a Logical Data Model is realized in a specific data store: data types, tables/files, indexing, partitioning, compression and physical history mechanisms. Explanation The physical model is where technology enters. Choices here should be traceable to logical and information-level requirements, e.g. a System-Versioned History Table realizing a transaction-time requirement. Distinctions - Versus Logical Data Model: logical says what structure , physical says how it is stored . - Versus technical implementation: deployment, pipelines and operations belong to the technical layer. Examples - A table customer with customer id BIGINT , clustered index, partitioned by region. - An Apache Iceberg table partitioned by day with snapshot retention of 30 days.

s: The meaning of a concept is defined and governed before, and independently of, its representation in information and data models.
x: Meaning Before Representation Statement The meaning of a concept shall be defined and governed before, and independently of, its representation in information and data models. Rationale When meaning is only implicit in models, code or column names, every consumer reinterprets it. Integration, migration and analytics then fail on semantic mismatch rather than on technology. Implications - A governed Business Concept exists (at least proposed ) before an entity representing it is approved. - Model elements link to concepts (Concept-to-Model Traceability). - Changing a definition is a semantic governance decision, not a model change (Decision Rights Model). Consequences - Positive: stable meaning across systems; cheaper integration and migration. - Negative: upfront effort; risk of analysis paralysis if applied dogmatically to low-value data. Applicability Shared, integrated and regulated data; master and reference data. Exceptions Local, single-application data without sharing ambitions. Prototypes, provided concepts are backfilled before production. Related Principles - Decisions Belong to Their Layer

s: A unit of business meaning — a thing, event, role or idea the organisation talks and decides about — identified by a preferred term and a governed definition.
x: Business Concept Definition A Business Concept is a unit of business meaning — a thing, event, role or idea the organisation talks and decides about — identified by a preferred term and a governed definition. Explanation Business concepts are the anchor of the chain Business Meaning → Governed Concept → Semantic Model → Information Model → Logical → Physical . A business concept becomes a governed concept once its definition has an owner, a status and approval (see Terminology Governance and Governance Lifecycle). A well-formed concept has: preferred term, definition, identity criterion ("when are two X the same X?"), synonyms, forbidden terms, broader/narrower concepts and an owner. Distinctions - A concept is not a term: one concept can have several terms (synonyms), and one term can denote several concepts (homonyms). Governance manages the mapping. - A concept is not an entity: an entity in a Data Model represents one or more concepts. Examples - "Customer", "Policy", "Claim", "Registration" in an insurance or public-sector context.

s: A governed list of approved terms, each with a defined meaning, used to label and classify information consistently.
x: Controlled Vocabulary Definition A Controlled Vocabulary is a governed list of approved terms, each with a defined meaning, used to label and classify information consistently. Explanation It is the simplest form of Semantic Model. Its key properties are: preferred terms, definitions, synonyms mapped to preferred terms, forbidden terms, and a change process. This knowledge base itself uses a controlled vocabulary ( 00-system/terminology/terminology.yaml ), governed by Terminology Governance. Distinctions - Versus Reference Data: reference data are the coded values used in data (e.g. NL , DE ); a controlled vocabulary governs terms and meanings . A code list is often the data realization of a controlled vocabulary. - Versus Taxonomy: no hierarchy required. Examples - The list of approved document types in a records management system.

s: A formal, explicit specification of concepts in a domain, their properties and relationships, and logical axioms, expressed so that machines can reason over it.
x: Ontology Definition An Ontology is a formal, explicit specification of the concepts in a domain, their properties and relationships, and logical axioms (e.g. disjointness, cardinality, equivalence), expressed so that machines can reason over it. Explanation Ontologies are the most formal form of Semantic Model. On the web-standards stack they are typically expressed in OWL 2 serialized as RDF 1.1. Their value lies in inference (deriving implicit facts), consistency checking and integration of heterogeneous sources through shared meaning. Distinctions - Versus Taxonomy: a taxonomy only has broader/narrower; an ontology has typed properties and axioms. - Versus Information Model: an ontology describes meaning under an open-world assumption; an information model describes the structure of records, typically under a closed-world assumption. Confusing the two leads to surprising validation behaviour. Examples - A domain ontology stating that every Vehicle Registration relates to exactly one Vehicle and that Natural Person and Legal Person are disjoint.

s: An explicit, governed representation of meaning — concepts, their definitions, identity criteria and semantic relationships such as specialization, generalization, part-whole and equivalence.
x: Semantic Model Definition A Semantic Model is an explicit, governed representation of meaning: concepts, their definitions and identity criteria, and semantic relationships such as specialization, generalization, part-whole and equivalence. Explanation The semantic model answers "what does something mean?" — deliberately separated from "how is that meaning represented in an information model?" (Information Model) and "how is it technically implemented?" (physical and technical layers). Semantic models range in formality: Form Formality Typical standard --- --- --- Controlled Vocabulary list of approved terms — Taxonomy hierarchy (broader/narrower) SKOS Thesaurus hierarchy + associative relations + synonyms SKOS Ontology classes, properties, axioms, reasoning OWL 2 on RDF 1.1 Choosing the formality is supported by Semantic Modeling Approach Decision Tree. Distinctions - Versus Conceptual Data Model: the conceptual model scopes data; the semantic model defines meaning, including concepts that never become data. - Semantic relationships (specializes, equivalent-to) are different from data relationships (foreign keys). Examples - "Natural Person" specializes "Party"; "Client" is equivalent to "Customer" in the sales vocabulary.

s: A hierarchical classification of concepts organised by broader/narrower relationships.
x: Taxonomy Definition A Taxonomy is a hierarchical classification of concepts organised by broader/narrower relationships. Explanation Taxonomies support classification, navigation and aggregation (e.g. product categories, document types). In SKOS, a taxonomy is a concept scheme with skos:broader / skos:narrower relations. Many reference data sets are taxonomies. Distinctions - Broader/narrower in a taxonomy is not necessarily class specialization ("is-a"): it may mean part-of or topical grouping. Ontologies make that distinction explicit. - Versus Controlled Vocabulary: a flat list without hierarchy. Examples - Product category hierarchy: Insurance → Non-life → Motor → Motor third-party liability.

s: Metadata is produced as part of designing and delivering data assets, preferably automatically, rather than documented afterwards.
x: Metadata Is Captured by Design Statement Metadata shall be produced as part of designing and delivering data assets — preferably automatically — rather than documented afterwards. Rationale Metadata documented afterwards is incomplete and quickly outdated. Metadata created in the delivery flow is current by construction. Implications - Definition of Done for data assets includes mandatory metadata (Mandatory Metadata Control). - Technical and lineage metadata are harvested from tools (Metadata Harvesting); business metadata is captured in the modeling workflow. Consequences - Positive: current catalog, reliable lineage. - Negative: tooling investment; requires metadata standards. Applicability All governed data assets. Exceptions Legacy assets are catalogued incrementally, prioritised by use and risk. Related Principles - Governance Is Embedded in Delivery

s: Metadata describing the origin of data and the path, transformations and dependencies through which it flows from source to consumption.
x: Data Lineage Definition Data Lineage is metadata describing the origin of data and the path, transformations and dependencies through which it flows from source to consumption. Explanation Lineage can be captured at several granularities (system, dataset, column) and in two flavours: - Design lineage : intended flows derived from mappings and models. - Runtime (operational) lineage : flows actually executed, captured from job execution. It supports impact analysis (see Architecture Change Process), root-cause analysis of Data Quality issues, regulatory traceability and migration reconciliation. Distinctions - Lineage vs provenance : provenance emphasises the origin and history of a specific data item; lineage emphasises flows between assets. Usage overlaps. - Lineage vs knowledge traceability (this knowledge base's source → decision → implementation chain): same idea applied to architecture knowledge instead of data. Examples - Report KPI "claims ratio" ← mart table ← warehouse fact ← two source systems, with transformation rules on each hop.

s: Data that describes other data or data-related assets — their meaning, structure, origin, quality, ownership, usage, security and processing.
x: Metadata Definition Metadata is data that describes other data or data-related assets — their meaning, structure, origin, quality, ownership, usage, security and processing. Explanation This knowledge base distinguishes nine metadata categories (spec §9). The categories overlap; a single attribute may serve several. Category Describes Examples Typical owner --- --- --- --- Business meaning and business context definitions, business rules, owner Data Owner / Data Steward Technical structure and storage schemas, data types, keys Data Custodian Operational runtime behaviour load times, row counts, job status platform operations Process processes that create/use data producing process, SLA process owner Semantic meaning formally concept links, ontology IRIs Semantic Architect Governance decisions and accountability status, approvals, policies Data Steward Quality fitness for use DQ rules, scores Data Steward Security protection classification, access policies Security Architect Lineage origin and flow source-to-target mappings Data Architect Architectural concerns: metadata ownership , lifecycle (metadata also goes through draft → approved → deprecated), standards (ISO IEC 11179 Metadata Registries), quality , repositories and APIs , and automation (Metadata Harvesting). See Metadata Management Reference Architecture. Distinctions - Metadata vs Reference Data: reference data are values used in business data; metadata describes data. - The distinction is role-based, not intrinsic:

s: The exercise of authority, control and shared decision-making over the management of data assets — who may decide what about data, on which basis, and how compliance is ensured.
x: Data Governance Definition Data Governance is the exercise of authority, control and shared decision-making over the management of data assets: who may decide what about data, on which basis, and how compliance is ensured. Explanation Data governance answers the questions of spec §10: - Who can decide? What can they decide? At which layer? - Based on which standards? What evidence is required? - Who approves? What is generated after approval? - How is the decision recorded and how can it be changed? These questions are answered structurally in Decision Rights Model, Governance Roles, Governance Lifecycle and the Architecture Governance Model. Governance is a first-class architectural layer , not a document produced at the end (Governance Is Embedded in Delivery; anti-pattern: Governance as Afterthought). Distinctions - Governance vs management : governance decides and oversees; data management executes. - Data governance vs architecture governance : data governance is about data assets; architecture governance is about architecture decisions and artifacts. They share roles and decision rights and are modeled together in Architecture Governance Model. Examples - A data owner approves the definition of "Active Customer"; a steward maintains the related quality rules.

s: The assignment of accountability for a defined set of data — its meaning, quality, access and lifecycle — to a business role with the authority to make decisions about it.
x: Data Ownership Definition Data Ownership is the assignment of accountability for a defined set of data — its meaning, quality, access and lifecycle — to a business role with the authority to make decisions about it. Explanation Ownership is accountability , not possession or technical administration. The owning role (Data Owner) decides; stewardship executes day-to-day care; the Data Custodian operates the technical environment. Ownership must be scoped: a data domain, a data set, a concept or a data product. Distinctions - Ownership ≠ custody: IT operating a database does not own the data. - Ownership ≠ authorship: the system or team creating data is not automatically its owner. Examples - The head of Claims owns claims data, including approval of the definition of "Open Claim".

s: The operational care for data on behalf of its owner — maintaining definitions, metadata, quality rules and issue resolution.
x: Data Stewardship Definition Data Stewardship is the operational care for data on behalf of its owner — maintaining definitions, metadata, quality rules and issue resolution. Explanation Stewards turn owner decisions into maintained reality: they propose definitions, monitor quality, triage issues and coordinate with custodians. Stewardship without ownership lacks authority; ownership without stewardship lacks execution. Distinctions - Business stewardship (meaning, rules) vs technical stewardship (structures, pipelines) — some organisations split the role. Examples - A steward maintains the rule "policy end date ≥ policy start date" and follows up violations.

s: Every governed data set, concept and architecture artifact has exactly one accountable owner with decision rights over it.
x: Data Has an Accountable Owner Statement Every governed data set, concept and architecture artifact shall have exactly one accountable owner with decision rights over it. Rationale Without an accountable owner, definitions drift, quality issues have no one to escalate to, and access decisions default to whoever administers the system. Implications - Ownership is recorded as metadata and checked by the Ownership Control. - Objects without owner cannot pass beyond proposed in the Governance Lifecycle (enforced by the validator for knowledge objects). - Owners must have authority matching their scope; see Decision Rights Model. Consequences - Positive: clear escalation, faster decisions, measurable accountability. - Negative: requires organisational commitment; nominal owners without time are a known failure mode. Applicability All shared and governed data; knowledge objects of this knowledge base. Exceptions Transient technical data (logs, temporary staging) may be owned collectively by the platform team. Exceptions are granted by the Data Governance body and recorded. Related Principles - Governance Is Embedded in Delivery - Each Data Element Has an Authoritative Source

s: Governance body that approves architecture decisions above the agreed threshold and decides on exceptions and cross-domain conflicts.
x: Architecture Board Purpose Provide a legitimate, cross-domain decision forum. Responsibilities - Approve significant ADRs. - Grant or refuse exceptions to principles. - Resolve cross-domain conflicts. - Monitor architecture compliance. Decision Rights Data architecture level above threshold; exceptions to principles. Inputs ADRs; impact analyses; review reports. Outputs Governance decisions (recorded with the Governance Decision Template). Required Competencies Composite: enterprise, data, security architects and business representatives. Escalation Paths Strategic issues → executive management. Related Governance Processes - Decision Rights Model - Architecture Change Process - Governance Lifecycle

s: Architect responsible for the realization of information in data structures, flows, history mechanisms and authoritative sources.
x: Data Architect Purpose Design data architecture that realizes information models within principles and standards. Responsibilities - Design logical models and data flows. - Decide history, integration and MDM approaches (with ADRs). - Designate authoritative sources. - Perform impact analysis. Decision Rights Data architecture level: logical structures, integration style, history mechanism; above threshold via Architecture Board. Inputs Information models; principles; platform capabilities. Outputs Logical models; ADRs; data flow designs. Required Competencies Data modeling; integration; temporal data; governance. Escalation Paths Cross-domain or principle exceptions → Architecture Board. Related Governance Processes - Decision Rights Model - Architecture Change Process - Governance Lifecycle

s: Technical role operating the storage, security and availability of data according to owner decisions.
x: Data Custodian Purpose Safeguard data technically without deciding on its meaning or use. Responsibilities - Operate databases and platforms. - Implement access controls as decided. - Run backup, recovery and retention jobs. - Provide technical metadata. Decision Rights Technical/formal level: operational configuration within standards. No rights on meaning or access policy. Inputs Access decisions; retention rules; platform standards. Outputs Operated environments; technical metadata; incident reports. Required Competencies Database/platform operations; security operations. Escalation Paths Policy conflicts → Data Owner; technical conflicts → Platform Architect. Related Governance Processes - Decision Rights Model - Architecture Change Process - Governance Lifecycle

s: Business role accountable for a defined set of data: its meaning, quality requirements, access and lifecycle.
x: Data Owner Purpose Carry accountability for owned data so decisions about it have a legitimate decider (Data Has an Accountable Owner). Responsibilities - Approve definitions of owned concepts. - Set quality requirements and accept residual quality risk. - Decide on access and sharing within policy. - Decide retention within legal limits, with the Privacy Specialist. Decision Rights Semantic level approver in the Decision Rights Model: meaning, quality requirements, access. No technical design rights. Inputs Proposals from Data Steward; impact analyses; quality reports. Outputs Approved definitions; quality requirements; access decisions. Required Competencies Business domain authority; data literacy; ability to weigh risk. Escalation Paths Cross-domain conflicts → Architecture Board or data governance council. Related Governance Processes - Decision Rights Model - Architecture Change Process - Governance Lifecycle

s: Operational role caring for data on behalf of the owner: definitions, metadata, quality rules and issue resolution.
x: Data Steward Purpose Turn owner decisions into maintained definitions, metadata and quality rules (Data Stewardship). Responsibilities - Draft and maintain definitions and synonyms. - Define and monitor quality rules; triage issues. - Maintain business metadata and reference data. - Coordinate with custodians on fixes. Decision Rights Proposes at the semantic level; decides on routine metadata maintenance within approved definitions. Inputs Owner decisions; quality measurements; user questions. Outputs Definitions (proposed); rules; issue resolutions; metadata. Required Competencies Domain knowledge; data quality methods; facilitation. Escalation Paths Unresolved issues → Data Owner. Related Governance Processes - Decision Rights Model - Architecture Change Process - Governance Lifecycle

s: Architect accountable for coherent architecture within one business domain, aligned with enterprise principles.
x: Domain Architect Purpose Keep a domain's architecture coherent and aligned. s: The degree to which data is fit for its intended uses, assessed against explicit requirements along defined quality dimensions.
x: Data Quality Definition Data Quality is the degree to which data is fit for its intended uses, assessed against explicit requirements along defined quality dimensions. Explanation Quality is relative to use : the same data can be adequate for trend reporting and inadequate for invoicing. Therefore quality requirements must be explicit, owned and measurable. Architecture contributes by: placing controls near the source (Quality Is Managed at the Source), building quality gates into flows, providing lineage for root-cause analysis, and designing models that prevent invalid states. Relevant standards include ISO IEC 25012 Data Quality Model (a quality model for data) and ISO 8000 Data Quality (a series on data quality and master data exchange). Distinctions - Data quality vs data validation : validation is one mechanism to check quality rules. - Data quality vs metadata quality : metadata has quality too (completeness of definitions, accuracy of lineage). Examples - "99.5% of active policies have a valid postal code" as a measurable requirement.

t: Quality Is Managed at the Source
s: Data quality issues are prevented and corrected as close as possible to where data is created, rather than repaired downstream.
x: Quality Is Managed at the Source Statement Data quality issues shall be prevented and corrected as close as possible to where data is created, rather than repaired downstream. Rationale Downstream repairs multiply (every consumer fixes the same problem differently) and hide root causes. Implications - Quality rules are owned by the producing domain and enforced at entry or at the producer interface (Data Contract). - Downstream quality gates detect and report, and route issues back to the source. Consequences - Positive: single fix, consistent data. - Negative: sources may be legacy or external systems that cannot be changed; then downstream correction is a documented, temporary exception. Applicability All shared data. Exceptions External data sources beyond organisational control; migration cleansing (Data Migration) as a one-time activity. Related Principles - Data Has an Accountable Owner

s: A named aspect of data quality — such as completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity or uniqueness — along which quality requirements are specified and measured.
x: Data Quality Dimension Definition A Data Quality Dimension is a named aspect of data quality along which requirements are specified and measured. Explanation Commonly used dimensions (lists differ between sources; this is common practice, not a single standard): Dimension Question --- --- Completeness Are required values present? Validity Do values conform to the defined domain/format? Accuracy Do values correctly represent reality? Consistency Do related values agree across records and systems? Timeliness Is data available and current when needed? Uniqueness Is each real-world entity represented once? ISO IEC 25012 Data Quality Model defines its own set of characteristics (inherent and system-dependent); names and definitions differ from the list above. Mapping between the two is an open task. Distinctions - A dimension is not a rule: rules are concrete, testable checks that measure a dimension. Examples - Rule "email matches pattern" measures validity ; "customer has exactly one active record" measures uniqueness . Open Questions - Map the common-practice dimensions to the ISO/IEC 25012 characteristics after verification against the standard text.

s: The integrated set of technical capabilities — storage, processing, integration, metadata, security and operations — on which data is stored, transformed and served.
x: Data Platform Definition A Data Platform is the integrated set of technical capabilities — storage, processing, integration, metadata, security and operations — on which data is stored, transformed and served. Explanation A platform is described first in terms of capabilities (technology-neutral), then realized by products. Typical capability groups: ingestion, storage, processing, serving, metadata and catalog, quality, security and access, orchestration, observability. Platform styles include operational databases, data warehouses, data lakes, lakehouses and streaming platforms. Layered Data Refinement is a common structuring pattern; Governed Analytical Data Platform is the reference architecture in this knowledge base. Distinctions - Platform vs Data Architecture: the platform is the realization substrate; architecture also covers meaning, models and governance. Examples - A cloud lakehouse using Apache Iceberg tables, an orchestration service and a catalog.

s: The combination of data from different sources, and its movement between systems, so that it can be used consistently for a shared purpose.
x: Data Integration Definition Data Integration is the combination of data from different sources, and its movement between systems, so that it can be used consistently for a shared purpose. Explanation Integration styles differ in latency, coupling, and where transformation happens: Style Latency Coupling Pattern --- --- --- --- Batch hours–days low runtime coupling Batch Extract-Transform-Load Change-based seconds–minutes medium Change Data Capture Event-based seconds domain events as contract Event Sourcing / event streaming Virtual query-time high runtime coupling Data Virtualization The semantic side of integration (do these fields mean the same?) is often the harder part; see Meaning Before Representation. Interfaces should be governed by explicit data contracts. Anti-pattern: Point-to-Point Integration Sprawl. Distinctions - Integration vs Data Migration: permanent vs transitional. Examples - Replicating customer changes from CRM to the data warehouse via CDC every minute.

s: The sequence of stages data passes through — creation or acquisition, storage, use, change, sharing, archiving and disposal — together with the rules governing each transition.
x: Data Lifecycle Definition The Data Lifecycle is the sequence of stages data passes through — creation or acquisition, storage, use, change, sharing, archiving and disposal — together with the rules governing each transition. Explanation Architecturally relevant lifecycle decisions: - Change : is history kept, and which kind? → Temporal Data Management. - Retention : how long must data be kept (legal, business), and how long may it be kept (privacy: storage limitation under GDPR)? - Archiving : when does data move to cheaper, less accessible storage, and can it still be queried? - Disposal : deletion, anonymisation or pseudonymisation; proving it happened. Retention obligations and deletion obligations can conflict (e.g. audit history vs. right to erasure). Such conflicts must be flagged and decided by the Data Owner with the Privacy Specialist, not silently resolved in design. Distinctions - Data lifecycle vs knowledge lifecycle : the Governance Lifecycle governs knowledge objects and architecture artifacts, not business data. Examples - Claims data: active use 2 years, archive 5 years, anonymise afterwards unless under litigation hold.

s: Requirements for history — which data, which time dimensions, which reconstruction questions and retention — are stated explicitly at the information layer before a history mechanism is chosen.
x: Historical Requirements Are Explicit Statement Requirements for history — which data, which time dimensions (valid time, transaction time), which reconstruction questions and which retention — shall be stated explicitly at the information layer before a history mechanism is chosen. Rationale History mechanisms are expensive to change after go-live. Choosing system versioning when the business needs valid-time corrections — or vice versa — is a common and costly mistake. Implications - Information models annotate history requirements per entity/attribute. - The mechanism is selected with Database History Pattern Decision Tree. Consequences - Positive: right-sized history, fewer rebuilds. - Negative: requires business stakeholders to answer temporal questions they rarely consider. Applicability Operational and analytical data subject to audit, correction or regulatory reconstruction. Exceptions Data without any history requirement is explicitly marked as "current-state only". Related Principles - Decisions Belong to Their Layer

s: The controlled, one-time or phased transfer of data from source systems to target systems, including mapping, transformation, cleansing, validation and reconciliation, with preserved meaning and traceability.
x: Data Migration Definition Data Migration is the controlled, one-time or phased transfer of data from source systems to target systems — including mapping, transformation, cleansing, validation and reconciliation — with preserved meaning and traceability. Explanation A migration is a data architecture problem before it is an ETL problem. It requires: 1. Semantic mapping : do source and target concepts mean the same? (see Semantic Model) 2. Profiling : what is actually in the source? (anti-pattern: Migration Without Data Profiling) 3. Mapping and transformation with documented Data Lineage. 4. Quality treatment : cleanse at source, in transit, or accept and flag. 5. Reconciliation : prove completeness and correctness (counts, sums, samples, business checks). 6. History : decide whether history migrates, and in which temporal form. 7. Cut-over approach : Big Bang Data Migration or Phased Data Migration. Distinctions - Migration vs integration : migration is transitional and ends; Data Integration is permanent. - Migration vs replication : replication keeps copies synchronized; it may be a technique used during a phased migration. Examples - Moving policy administration from a legacy mainframe to a package system in three product-line waves.

s: The consolidated, best-known version of a master data entity, assembled from one or more source records according to survivorship rules.
x: Golden Record Definition A Golden Record is the consolidated, best-known version of a master data entity, assembled from one or more source records according to matching and survivorship rules. Explanation Creating a golden record requires: identity resolution (match), linking source records (cross-reference), survivorship rules per attribute (which source wins, recency, completeness), and lineage back to contributing records. It is best-known , not true : its quality depends on sources and rules. Distinctions - A golden record is not necessarily physically stored: in a registry-style hub it can be virtual. Examples - One customer record combining the address from the CRM (most recent) and the birth date from the policy system (most trusted).

s: The data about core business entities — such as parties, products, locations and assets — that is shared across processes and systems and provides context to transactions.
x: Master Data Definition Master Data is the data about core business entities — parties, products, locations, assets — that is shared across processes and systems and provides context to transactions. Explanation Master data is characterised by: sharing across many processes, relatively slow change, high impact of errors, and identity problems (the same customer in five systems). Master data management (MDM) addresses identity resolution, consolidation into a Golden Record, distribution, and governance. The architecture style (registry, consolidation, coexistence, centralized) is selected with Master Data Architecture Decision Tree and realized by a Master Data Hub. Distinctions - Master data vs Reference Data: reference data classifies (code lists: country, currency, status); master data describes business entities. Reference data is usually smaller, more stable, and often externally defined. The two are frequently confused; they are linked with distinct-from . - Master data vs transactional data : transactions (orders, claims) reference master data. Examples - Customer, supplier, product, employee, site.

s: Sets of permissible values — codes and their meanings — used to classify or categorise other data, often defined by external bodies and shared across systems.
x: Reference Data Definition Reference Data are sets of permissible values — codes and their meanings — used to classify or categorise other data. They are often defined by external bodies (e.g. country and currency codes) and shared across systems. Explanation Reference data typically realizes a Controlled Vocabulary or Taxonomy at the data level. Architectural concerns: authoritative source per code list, versioning and validity periods of codes, mappings between code lists, and distribution (Reference Data Hub). Codes change over time: a code can be retired while historical data still uses it. Code lists therefore need their own temporal management. Distinctions - vs Master Data: see there. - vs Metadata: reference data values appear in business data. Examples - Country codes, currency codes, claim status codes, product categories.

s: The pull-request based process by which a proposed change to the knowledge graph is validated, reviewed, decided per governance level, recorded, merged and published.
x: Knowledge Change Review Process Purpose Turn "a proposed change to the governed architecture knowledge graph" (a pull request) into an audited decision. Machine-readable: 00-system/governance/review-process.yaml . Trigger A pull request from a feature/ , fix/ , schema/ , taxonomy/ or governance/ branch. Steps 1. Submit — contributor opens the PR with the template; discloses AI assistance. 2. Validate — workflows validate-schema, validate-knowledge, validate-links, governance-check; report in the job summary. 3. Triage — domain owner assigns a reviewer, confirms required governance levels. 4. Content review — reviewer applies the Knowledge Quality Model. 5. Level decisions — semantic → information model → data architecture → technical (Decision Rights Model). 6. Record — governance record added in the same PR. 7. Merge — after code-owner review and green checks. 8. Publish — release tag and publication record. Inputs Pull request, validation report, governance levels required. Outputs Merged change, governance record, audit trail. Roles Contributor, reviewer, domain owner, approvers per level, code owners, publisher — see 00-system/governance/roles.yaml .

s: An approval contains one decision for each governance level the object's layers require - semantic, information model, data architecture, technical - never a single combined approval.
x: Separate Decision per Governance Level Rule Required levels are derived from the object's layer ( decision-rights.yaml layer levels ). The governance record must hold a positive decision per level, by an approver role of that level (E095, E097). Rationale "What does it mean?", "how is it represented?", "how does it participate in the architecture?" and "how is it technically represented?" are different questions with different deciders (Decision Rights Model). Scope All approvals. Enforcement Automated: E095, E097. Machine definition: AR-002, AR-004. Exceptions None; small teams may have one person in several roles, but the decisions are still recorded separately.

s: Nobody approves a change they proposed or an object they own.
x: Separation of Duties in Approval Rule A decider in a governance record is neither the record's proposed by nor the object's owner (or a member of the owner role). Rationale Four-eyes principle; prevents self-approval. Scope All governance records. Enforcement Automated: E096. Machine definition: AR-003. Exceptions None.

s: An object may only be approved, published, implemented, deprecated or retired when an append-only governance record establishes that transition for its current version.

The validator (E092) rejects any object in an approved state without a governance record for its current version in 00-system/governance/records/ ; the governance-check workflow (G04) requires the record to be added in the same pull request. Rationale A contributor must not be able to make knowledge authoritative by editing one field. Approval is a recorded decision by people with decision rights. Scope All knowledge objects.
