s: Significant architecture decisions are recorded with their context, options and rationale, and are traceable from source knowledge to implementation.
x: Architecture Decisions Are Traceable Statement Significant architecture decisions shall be recorded with their context, options and rationale, and be traceable along the chain Source → Knowledge → Decision → Architecture → Implementation . Rationale Unrecorded decisions are re-debated, silently reversed, or cannot be defended to auditors. Implications - Decisions use the ADR structure (see 00-system/templates/ADR Template.md ). - Decisions link to the patterns and principles considered and to the architectures they affect. Consequences - Positive: institutional memory, auditable architecture. - Negative: documentation effort; mitigated by lightweight ADRs. Applicability Decisions that are costly to reverse, cross team boundaries or affect governed data. Exceptions Easily reversible local decisions. Related Principles - Decisions Belong to Their Layer

s: Governance controls are built into the delivery workflow as automated and review steps, rather than applied as a separate documentation phase at the end.
x: Governance Is Embedded in Delivery Statement Governance controls shall be built into the delivery workflow as automated checks and review steps, rather than applied as a separate documentation phase at the end. Rationale End-of-process governance finds problems when they are most expensive to fix and turns governance into paperwork. Implications - Controls have triggers inside the workflow (pull request, model check-in, deployment). - Automated validation produces VALID / WARNING / BLOCKING ERROR, as this repository does with 00-system/validation/dakb.py . Consequences - Positive: earlier feedback, less bureaucracy, evidence generated automatically. - Negative: requires tooling and explicit, machine-checkable rules. Applicability Architecture and data delivery; this knowledge base itself. Exceptions Governance decisions requiring human judgement remain human (Knowledge Repository Governance); automation provides evidence, not approval. Related Principles - Metadata Is Captured by Design

s: Open table format for large analytic datasets providing snapshots, time travel, schema evolution and hidden partitioning on file/object storage.
x: Apache Iceberg Purpose Reliable, engine-independent tables on object storage for lakehouse architectures. Capabilities - Snapshot-based commits with atomic table changes. - Time travel to prior snapshots (technical, transaction-time-like). - Schema evolution and partition evolution; hidden partitioning. - Access from multiple processing engines via catalogs. Limitations - Snapshot time travel is bounded by snapshot expiration and is not a business history model (no valid time). - Requires a catalog and maintenance (compaction, snapshot expiry). Architecture Role Storage/table layer of a Data Platform; physical layer of Layered Data Refinement. Applicable Patterns Layered Data Refinement, Change Data Capture targets, Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2 tables. Alternatives Other open table formats; warehouse-native storage. Integration Engines and catalogs vary; verify per environment. Verification Notes No version pinned; capabilities stated at a general level.

s: Microsoft SQL Server / Azure SQL feature that implements system-versioned (transaction-time) tables with automatic history tables and FOR SYSTEM_TIME queries.
x: SQL Server Temporal Tables Purpose Automatic retention of prior row versions for point-in-time analysis and audit. Capabilities - System-versioned tables with period columns and a linked history table. - Query clauses FOR SYSTEM TIME AS OF FROM … TO BETWEEN … AND CONTAINED IN ALL . - History retention policies (availability depends on version/platform). Limitations - Transaction time only; application-time (valid-time) periods from the SQL standard are not provided natively, so a Bitemporal Data Model needs application-maintained valid time. - Some schema changes require temporarily disabling system versioning. Architecture Role Physical implementation of the System-Versioned History Table pattern for Temporal Data Management. Applicable Patterns System-Versioned History Table; transaction-time half of Bitemporal Data Model. Alternatives Other DBMSs with system versioning; trigger-based history tables; Change Data Capture into an archive. Integration History tables can be exposed to analytical platforms via CDC or batch extraction. Verification Notes Version-specific capabilities to be verified against current vendor documentation.

s: Open-source, log-based change data capture platform, commonly deployed on Kafka Connect, emitting row-level change events from databases.
x: Debezium Purpose Capture database changes from transaction logs and publish them as event streams. Capabilities - Connectors for several relational and document databases. - Initial snapshots followed by streaming changes, including deletes. - Deployable as Kafka Connect connectors or as a standalone server for other sinks. Limitations - Emits physical row changes; business meaning must be added downstream or via a Data Contract. - Dependent on source log configuration and retention. Architecture Role Technical implementation of Change Data Capture in Data Integration. Applicable Patterns Change Data Capture, synchronisation within Phased Data Migration. Alternatives Vendor CDC tools; database-native replication. Integration Typically: source DB → Debezium → Kafka topics → sink connectors / stream processing → platform. Verification Notes Supported connectors and deployment modes to be verified per version.

s: Reference architecture for an analytical data platform with layered refinement, embedded quality gates, metadata and lineage, and governance built in.
x: Governed Analytical Data Platform Purpose Provide a reusable structure for analytical platforms that serve trusted, governed data to BI, analytics and data science. Scope Ingestion to consumption for analytical use. Excludes operational (OLTP) systems and ML model serving. Context Multiple sources, multiple consumers, regulatory reporting, need for history. Architecture Components Component Responsibility Pattern --- --- --- Ingestion acquire data with lineage Change Data Capture, Batch Extract-Transform-Load Raw layer immutable landing, replay Layered Data Refinement Conformed layer cleansed, integrated, historized, concept-linked Bitemporal Data Model or Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2, Concept-to-Model Traceability Consumption layer purpose-built models dimensional marts Quality rule evaluation at promotion Data Quality Gate Metadata & catalog technical, business, lineage metadata Metadata Harvesting, Metadata Management Reference Architecture Security classification-driven access Security Classification Control Interfaces - Producer interfaces governed by data contracts. - Consumer interfaces: SQL, semantic/BI layer, APIs. - Metadata API to the catalog. Data Flows Source → raw (as received) → conformed (integrated + history) → consumption (fit for use). Issues flow back to source owners. Governance Owners per data product/layer; contracts at ingestion; quality rules owned by producers (Quality Is Managed at the Source); decisions recorded as ADRs. Security Classification

s: Periodically extract data sets from sources, transform them and load them into a target, in scheduled batches (ETL or ELT).
x: Batch Extract-Transform-Load Problem Data from several sources must be combined and made available in a target on a predictable schedule. Context Analytical platforms, reporting, periodic interfaces, migrations. Forces - Simplicity and robustness vs. latency. - Source load windows. Solution Scheduled jobs extract full or incremental data sets, transform them (before load: ETL; after load in the target: ELT), and load them into the target with restartable, idempotent steps. Architecture Advantages - Simple, mature, easy to reason about and reconcile. - Low runtime coupling. Disadvantages - Latency equals schedule. - Incremental extraction without CDC may miss deletes. Risks - Growing batch windows; silent partial loads without reconciliation. When to Use - Latency of hours is acceptable; large set-based transformations. When Not to Use - Near-real-time requirements → Change Data Capture. Alternatives Change Data Capture, Data Virtualization. Examples - Nightly load of finance ledgers into a warehouse. Related Decisions - Select Data Integration Style

s: Migrate all data in a single cut-over event after rehearsals, switching all users from source to target at once.
x: Big Bang Data Migration Problem Data must move to a new system, and coexistence is impractical. Context Moderate volumes, tightly coupled data, acceptable downtime window. Forces - Simplicity vs. concentrated risk. Solution Build and rehearse the full migration repeatedly (dress rehearsals with production copies), reconcile each rehearsal, then execute once in a planned window with a go/no-go decision and rollback plan. Architecture Advantages - No coexistence; simpler design; shorter total duration. Disadvantages - All risk concentrated in one event. Risks - Downtime overrun; rollback infeasible after go-live transactions. When to Use - Data cannot be partitioned; downtime acceptable; rehearsals feasible. When Not to Use - Mission-critical systems without downtime tolerance. Alternatives Phased Data Migration. Examples - Weekend cut-over of an HR system after three rehearsals. Related Decisions - Select Data Migration Approach

s: Record both valid time and transaction time for each fact so that any past state can be reconstructed as it was true and as it was known.
x: Bitemporal Data Model Problem The business must answer "what was true at time T?" and "what did we believe at time T′ about time T?" — for example after retroactive corrections. Context Regulated domains (insurance, finance, public registers, HR/payroll) where corrections are backdated and decisions must be reproducible. Forces - Retroactive corrections must not destroy what was previously known. - Queries must stay understandable. - Storage and write complexity grow with two time dimensions. Solution Every versioned fact carries two periods: a valid-time period [valid from, valid to) maintained by the application, and a transaction-time period [recorded from, recorded to) maintained by the system. Updates never overwrite: they close the current transaction-time period and insert new rows. Architecture Queries filter on both periods ("as of valid date V, as known at T"). The information model states which entities/attributes are bitemporal; the physical model may combine an application-time period with a System-Versioned History Table. Advantages - Full reproducibility of past decisions and reports. - Clean handling of backdated corrections. Disadvantages - Complex writes (period splitting) and queries. - Higher storage. - Many tools and developers are unfamiliar with it. Risks - Incorrect period maintenance creates gaps or overlaps; needs constraints and tests. - Uniform application to all entities over-engineers the model. When to Use - Retroactive changes are common and re

s: Detect inserts, updates and deletes in a source database (typically from its transaction log) and propagate them as a change stream to targets.
x: Change Data Capture Problem Targets need source changes with low latency, without heavy load on the source and without modifying the source application. Context Replication to warehouses/lakes, cache invalidation, phased migrations. Forces - Low latency vs. source impact. - Technical change events vs. business meaning. Solution Read the database transaction log (or triggers/timestamps as weaker variants), emit ordered change events per row, and apply them to targets. Architecture Advantages - Near-real-time; low source impact (log-based). - Captures deletes (log-based). Disadvantages - Exposes the source's physical schema as an implicit contract. - Row-level changes lack business intent. Risks - Source schema changes break consumers → mitigate with a Data Contract. - Log retention and connector outages cause gaps; needs reconciliation. When to Use - Low-latency replication; Phased Data Migration synchronization. When Not to Use - Consumers need business events → Event Sourcing / domain events. - Daily latency suffices → Batch Extract-Transform-Load. Alternatives Batch Extract-Transform-Load, Event Sourcing, Data Virtualization. Examples - Streaming CRM customer changes into a lakehouse bronze layer (Layered Data Refinement). Related Decisions - Select Data Integration Style

s: Link every model element at each layer to the governed concept it represents and to the model element it realizes, so meaning and impact can be traced across layers.
x: Concept-to-Model Traceability Problem Nobody can tell which business concept a table or column represents, or which models are affected when a definition changes. Context Organisations with governed business concepts and models at multiple layers. Forces - Traceability value vs. maintenance effort. Solution Maintain explicit links: physical column → realizes → logical attribute → realizes → information attribute → represents → concept . Store the links as metadata (e.g. concept IRIs in model annotations) and validate them automatically. Architecture Advantages - Impact analysis of definition changes; shared meaning in integration and migration. Disadvantages - Needs tooling and discipline. Risks - Links created mechanically without semantic review. When to Use - Governed, shared or regulated data. When Not to Use - Throw-away prototypes. Alternatives Glossary-only linking (catalog term to column) — weaker, skips intermediate layers. Examples - Column klant.ingangsdatum linked to concept "Customer Since Date" through the information model. Related Decisions - Select Semantic Modeling Formalism

s: Make the interface between a data producer and its consumers an explicit, versioned, owned agreement covering schema, semantics, quality and service levels, and enforce it automatically.
x: Data Contract Problem Consumers depend on data whose structure and meaning the producer changes without notice. Context Multiple teams producing and consuming data (data mesh, microservices, platforms). Forces - Producer autonomy vs. consumer stability. - Formality vs. speed. Solution Define per data interface a contract: schema, semantics (links to concepts), quality rules, freshness/SLA, owner, version and change policy. Validate it in the producer's pipeline and at ingestion (Data Quality Gate). Architecture Advantages - Breaking changes become visible and negotiated. - Quality ownership sits with the producer. Disadvantages - Governance overhead; contract sprawl. Risks - Contracts that cover schema only, not meaning, give false assurance. When to Use - Cross-team data interfaces with several consumers. When Not to Use - Single-team, single-consumer pipelines. Alternatives Schema registry only (weaker), shared canonical model. Examples - A "Policy Issued" dataset contract with fields, definitions, completeness ≥ 99.9% and 1-hour freshness. Related Decisions - Select Data Integration Style

s: Validate data against explicit quality rules at defined points in a data flow and block, quarantine or flag data that fails, with evidence recorded.
x: Data Quality Gate Problem Bad data propagates silently to consumers and is discovered late. Context Pipelines between layers, producer interfaces, migrations. Forces - Blocking protects consumers but can halt the business. - Rule maintenance effort. Solution At each gate, evaluate owned rules (per dimension) with a severity: blocking (stop/quarantine), warning (pass and flag), info . Record results as quality metadata and route issues to the owning steward. Architecture This repository applies the same pattern to knowledge: VALID / WARNING / BLOCKING ERROR. Advantages - Early detection; measurable quality; evidence for audits. Disadvantages - Rule sprawl; false positives. Risks - Gates that only warn become ignored. When to Use - Any promotion to a trusted layer; migration loads. When Not to Use - Exploratory sandboxes. Alternatives Downstream reconciliation only (weaker). Examples - Blocking rule "policy has exactly one holder"; warning rule "email present". Related Decisions - Select Data Migration Approach

s: Provide an integrated, queryable view over multiple sources at query time without physically copying the data.
x: Data Virtualization Problem Consumers need a combined view of data from several systems, but copying is undesirable (latency, duplication, privacy). Context Exploratory analytics, low-volume operational lookups, regulated data that must stay in place. Forces - Freshness and no duplication vs. performance and source load. Solution A virtualization layer exposes logical views that are translated at query time into queries on the underlying sources, with optional caching. Architecture Advantages - Current data; no copies to govern. - Fast to set up for prototypes. Disadvantages - Performance depends on sources; complex joins across sources are slow. - No history unless sources keep it. Risks - Operational sources overloaded by analytical queries. When to Use - Low volume, high freshness, data must not be copied. When Not to Use - Heavy analytics or history requirements → Batch Extract-Transform-Load into a platform. Alternatives Batch Extract-Transform-Load, Change Data Capture. Examples - A combined customer view for a service desk over CRM and billing. Related Decisions - Select Data Integration Style

s: Persist every state change as an immutable domain event in an append-only log and derive current and past states by replaying events.
x: Event Sourcing Problem The reason and sequence of changes matter, not just resulting states; state must be reconstructable and changes shared with other systems. Context Domain-driven systems with rich business events; audit-heavy processes. Forces - Complete audit and replay versus query simplicity. - Event schema evolution over long periods. Solution Store each change as an immutable event (e.g. AddressChanged ) in an append-only store. Current state is a projection built by replaying events; other projections serve queries and other systems. Architecture Advantages - Full history with intent. - Natural integration via events. - New read models can be derived retroactively. Disadvantages - Querying current state requires projections. - Event versioning and replay complexity. Risks - Events designed as CRUD deltas lose business meaning. - Personal data in immutable logs complicates erasure obligations (GDPR). When to Use - Business events are first-class; audit with intent is required. When Not to Use - Simple CRUD applications; teams without event modeling experience. Alternatives System-Versioned History Table, Bitemporal Data Model, Change Data Capture (for integration only). Examples - A registration system storing VehicleRegistered , OwnerChanged , RegistrationSuspended . Related Decisions - Select Historical Data Strategy - Select Data Integration Style

s: Organise an analytical platform in successive layers — raw, conformed, consumption-ready — each with explicit quality, modeling and governance guarantees.
x: Layered Data Refinement Problem Analytical platforms mix raw and curated data, so consumers cannot tell what is trustworthy and pipelines become entangled. Context Data lakes, lakehouses and warehouses serving several consumers. Forces - Keep raw data for replay/audit vs. offer curated, governed data. - Number of layers vs. latency and cost. Solution Define layers with contracts: Layer Also called Content Guarantee --- --- --- --- Raw bronze, landing source data as received, append-only completeness of receipt, lineage Conformed silver, integrated cleansed, integrated, historized, linked to concepts quality rules passed, semantics mapped Consumption gold, marts purpose-built models (e.g. dimensional) fit for a specific use, owned Promotion between layers passes a Data Quality Gate. Architecture Advantages - Replayability; clear trust levels; separation of concerns. Disadvantages - Data duplication; added latency. Risks - Layers named but without guarantees ("gold" that nobody owns). - Semantic integration postponed indefinitely in the conformed layer. When to Use - Multi-source, multi-consumer analytical platforms. When Not to Use - Single-source operational reporting; virtualization suffices. Alternatives Classic staging–warehouse–mart; Data Virtualization. Examples - Claims data landed raw hourly, conformed with a bitemporal policy model, served as a claims mart. Related Decisions - Select Historical Data Strategy

s: Manage shared master data entities in a hub that performs identity resolution, maintains golden records and cross-references, and distributes master data, in registry, consolidation, coexistence or centralized style.
x: Master Data Hub Problem The same business entity exists in many systems with conflicting values and identifiers. Context Customer, product or supplier data maintained in several applications. Forces - Source system autonomy vs. central authority. - Real-time consistency vs. implementation effort. Solution A hub matches records, keeps cross-references, applies survivorship to build a Golden Record and distributes it. Four common implementation styles: Style Authoring Golden record Invasiveness --- --- --- --- Registry in sources virtual (index + cross-ref) low Consolidation in sources physical, read-only in hub (for analytics) low–medium Coexistence in sources and hub physical, synchronised back medium–high Centralized (transaction) in hub only physical, authoritative high Architecture Advantages - Single identity; consistent attributes; reusable services. Disadvantages - Organisational change; hub becomes critical infrastructure. Risks - Technology-first MDM without ownership and definitions fails. When to Use - Shared entities with material cost of inconsistency. When Not to Use - Entities used by one system only. Alternatives Per-attribute authoritative sources with plain integration; Reference Data Hub for code lists. Examples - Consolidation-style customer hub feeding the analytics platform, later evolving to coexistence. Related Decisions - Select Master Data Hub Style

s: Automatically extract technical, operational and lineage metadata from source systems, pipelines and tools into a central metadata repository on a schedule or event basis.
x: Metadata Harvesting Problem Manually maintained catalogs are incomplete and outdated. Context Heterogeneous landscapes with databases, pipelines and BI tools. Forces - Automation breadth vs. metadata depth (business meaning cannot be harvested). Solution Connectors read schemas, job definitions, query logs and run events; normalise into the repository's metamodel; link harvested technical assets to curated business metadata (concepts, owners). Architecture Advantages - Current technical metadata and lineage at low marginal cost. Disadvantages - Connector coverage gaps; lineage through custom code is hard. Risks - A catalog full of harvested but unexplained assets ("metadata swamp"). When to Use - More than a handful of systems; lineage required. When Not to Use - Very small landscapes where curated documentation suffices. Alternatives Manual curation; metadata-driven development (generate pipelines from metadata). Examples - Nightly harvest of warehouse schemas plus runtime lineage events from orchestration. Related Decisions - None yet; candidate decision "Metadata Architecture" (see recommended next batch).

s: Migrate data in successive waves (by product, region or entity), with source and target coexisting and synchronised during the transition.
x: Phased Data Migration Problem A single cut-over is too risky or impossible within the available downtime. Context Large or business-critical migrations; systems that can coexist. Forces - Risk reduction vs. cost and complexity of coexistence. Solution Partition the data into waves. For each wave: migrate, reconcile, switch users/processes. Keep source and target synchronised (e.g. Change Data Capture or dual write) for data shared across waves. Architecture Advantages - Smaller blast radius; learning between waves. Disadvantages - Coexistence complexity; longer total duration; temporary interfaces. Risks - Synchronisation errors; wave boundaries that cut through shared entities. When to Use - High risk, limited downtime, separable data. When Not to Use - Tightly coupled data that cannot be partitioned; small volumes. Alternatives Big Bang Data Migration. Examples - Migrating policies product line by product line. Related Decisions - Select Data Migration Approach

s: Maintain code lists centrally with versions, validity periods and cross-list mappings, and distribute them to consuming systems.
x: Reference Data Hub Problem Code lists are copied into every application and drift apart. Context Many systems using the same classifications (status codes, product types, external code lists). Forces - Local extensions vs. central consistency. Solution One governed store per code list with: code, label(s), definition, validity period, version, mapping to other lists and to vocabulary concepts. Distribution via API, files or events; consumers validate against it. Architecture Advantages - Consistent classification; controlled change. Disadvantages - Additional component; synchronisation latency. Risks - Retiring a code without validity periods breaks historical data. When to Use - Code lists shared by several systems or used in regulatory reporting. When Not to Use - Truly local, application-internal enumerations. Alternatives Master Data Hub (if the tool covers reference data), static published files. Examples - Claim status codes with mapping to a regulator's reporting codes. Related Decisions - Select Master Data Hub Style

s: In a dimensional model, preserve history of dimension attributes by inserting a new dimension row with its own surrogate key and effective period for each change.
x: Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2 Problem Analytical facts must be reported against the dimension attributes that were valid when the fact occurred (e.g. customer segment at sale time). Context Dimensional data warehouses and marts. Forces - Reports need both "as was" and sometimes "as is" views. - Fact tables should join simply to dimensions. Solution On change of a tracked attribute, expire the current dimension row ( effective to , is current = false ) and insert a new row with a new surrogate key. Facts reference the surrogate key valid at the fact's time. Architecture Advantages - Simple, well-known, tool-supported. - Fast "as was" reporting. Disadvantages - Typically single time dimension; backdated corrections are awkward. - Dimension growth with volatile attributes. Risks - Tracking too many attributes explodes dimension size. - Late-arriving facts can bind to the wrong version. When to Use - Analytical history of descriptive attributes. When Not to Use - Operational reconstruction or legal reproducibility → Bitemporal Data Model. Alternatives SCD Type 1 (overwrite), SCD Type 4 (history table), Bitemporal Data Model. Examples - Sales by customer segment as the segment was at sale time. Related Decisions - Select Historical Data Strategy

s: Let the database automatically keep every prior version of a row, with system-maintained transaction-time periods, in an associated history table.
x: System-Versioned History Table Problem Operational data is updated in place, but users or auditors need to see what the data looked like at a past point in (system) time. Context Operational databases where history of recorded state is needed and valid-time corrections are rare or not required. Forces - Applications should not have to write history themselves. - History must be tamper-resistant. - Current-state queries must remain fast. Solution Each row carries a system-maintained period ( sys start , sys end ). On update/delete, the DBMS moves the prior version to a history table. Queries use "as of" syntax to read past states. Architecture Advantages - Transparent to applications. - Consistent, DBMS-enforced transaction time. - Standardized in SQL (SQL Standard Temporal Support). Disadvantages - Captures transaction time only; backdated business corrections are not represented as such. - History growth needs retention management. Risks - Mistaking system time for business validity leads to wrong reconstructions. - Schema changes on temporal tables can be constrained by the DBMS. When to Use - "What did the database say at time T?" is the key question. When Not to Use - Retroactive valid-time corrections must be reconstructable → Bitemporal Data Model. Alternatives Bitemporal Data Model, Event Sourcing, application-maintained audit tables. Examples - Reconstructing a customer's contact details as stored at the moment a letter was sent. Related Decisions - Select Historical

s: Governance is applied as a documentation and approval step at the end of delivery, instead of being embedded in the architecture and workflow.
x: Governance as Afterthought Problem Architecture review and data governance happen after design is finished, as a gate to "get the stamp". Symptoms - Review boards reject or wave through finished work. - Documentation written after go-live. - Governance perceived as bureaucracy. Root Causes - Governance modeled as documents rather than decisions; no decision rights per layer. Consequences - Late, expensive rework or accepted non-compliance. Detection - Compare decision dates to implementation dates; count ADRs created after deployment. Remediation - Define decision rights per layer (Decision Rights Model); embed controls in the workflow (Architecture Change Process); automate evidence. Alternative Patterns Architecture Change Process, Data Contract. When It May Be Acceptable Never as a default; post-hoc review is acceptable for emergency changes, with retroactive recording.

s: The meaning of data exists only implicitly in column names, application code or people's heads, instead of in governed definitions.
x: Implicit Semantics Problem Data meaning is inferred from names ( status , date1 , klant type ) and code, never stated. Symptoms - Recurring discussions about "what this field really means". - Two reports with the same KPI name and different numbers. - Migration mappings based on column names only. Root Causes - Delivery pressure; no semantic role; modeling starts at the physical layer (Physical-Model-First Design). Consequences - Integration errors, misreporting, costly migrations, regulatory risk. Detection - Sample columns of key tables: can a definition, owner and concept link be found for each? Coverage below an agreed threshold indicates the anti-pattern. Remediation - Introduce governed concepts for high-value data first; link models (Concept-to-Model Traceability); require definitions in data contracts. Alternative Patterns Concept-to-Model Traceability, Data Contract. When It May Be Acceptable Local, short-lived data with a single producer and consumer.

s: Migration mappings are designed from documentation and schema only, without profiling the actual source data.
x: Migration Without Data Profiling Problem Mappings assume documented behaviour; actual data contains undocumented codes, overloaded fields and invalid combinations. Symptoms - Load failures late in the project; manual fix lists; reconciliation that never balances. Root Causes - Schedule pressure; source access restrictions; overconfidence in documentation. Consequences - Delays, data loss, corrupted history in the target. Detection - No profiling results linked to mapping specifications. Remediation - Profile early (value distributions, nulls, patterns, referential integrity); revise mappings; add quality gates to rehearsals. Alternative Patterns Phased Data Migration (learning between waves), Big Bang Data Migration with repeated rehearsals. When It May Be Acceptable Tiny, fully understood data sets.

s: One attribute carries different meanings depending on context, record type or time, instead of separate, well-defined attributes.
x: Overloaded Attribute Problem A field such as date 1 holds the start date for policies and the birth date for persons; code means different code lists per record type. Symptoms - Interpretation depends on another column's value. - Many CASE expressions in consumers. - Quality rules that differ per record type for the same field. Root Causes - Avoiding schema changes; generic "flexible" designs; reuse of legacy fields. Consequences - Ambiguous reports; failed validations; migration mapping errors. Detection - Profiling: value distributions differing strongly by record type; comments like "if type = X then …". Remediation - Split into distinct attributes linked to distinct concepts; during migration, map per context. Alternative Patterns Concept-to-Model Traceability. When It May Be Acceptable Generic key-value stores where the key explicitly identifies the meaning (then it is metadata-driven, not overloaded).

s: Data structures are designed directly as database tables, skipping the conceptual, semantic and information layers.
x: Physical-Model-First Design Problem Design starts with CREATE TABLE . Meaning, scope and history requirements are implicit in the physical design. Symptoms - No conceptual or information model exists; ER diagrams are reverse-engineered. - Technology choices dictate business definitions. Root Causes - Developer-led delivery without architecture roles; tools that start physical. Consequences - Semantic drift; hard-to-change history mechanisms; poor reuse. Detection - Models exist only at physical level; no concept links. Remediation - Introduce lightweight conceptual and information models for shared data; add traceability. Alternative Patterns Concept-to-Model Traceability. When It May Be Acceptable Technical/internal data with no semantic sharing; prototypes that will be redesigned.

s: Systems are integrated through many individually built point-to-point interfaces, each with its own mapping, semantics and quality handling.
x: Point-to-Point Integration Sprawl Problem Every new need creates another direct interface; the number of interfaces grows towards n × (n−1). Symptoms - Nobody has an overview of interfaces. - The same data transformed differently in several interfaces. - Changes in one system break unknown consumers. Root Causes - Project-by-project funding; no integration architecture or authoritative sources. Consequences - High change cost; inconsistent data; fragile landscape. Detection - Interface inventory and lineage show multiple copies of the same entity with different transformations. Remediation - Designate authoritative sources; introduce hubs or shared platforms; govern interfaces with contracts. Alternative Patterns Master Data Hub, Change Data Capture to a shared platform, Data Contract. When It May Be Acceptable Very few systems with stable interfaces.

t: Declare Epistemic Status on Every Object
s: Every knowledge object declares epistemic_status (verified fact, external standard, common practice, expert interpretation, recommendation, hypothesis, experimental) and confidence, and leaves sources empty when no verified source exists.
x: Declare Epistemic Status on Every Object Context Spec §3.5 requires distinguishing facts, standards, practice, interpretation, recommendation, hypothesis and experiment. Spec §20/§31 forbid invented sources. Problem How to make uncertainty explicit and machine-checkable? Options 1. Object-level epistemic status + confidence fields. 2. Inline claim-level annotations only. 3. Both. Evaluation Criteria Simplicity, machine-readability, granularity. Trade-offs - Object-level is coarse: a pattern may mix common practice with recommendations. Claim-level is precise but heavy. Decision Proposed: option 1 now, claim-level annotation later where needed (e.g. "Open Questions" sections and explicit "flagged" statements in body text). Consequences - In release 0.1, almost all objects have sources: [] and confidence reflecting the author's judgement. Standards objects carry a "Verification Notes" section: bibliographic details must be checked by a human before approval. Assumptions - A human reviewer will attach verified sources during review. Constraints - The LLM never invents sources. Related Architecture - Knowledge Quality Model

t: Separate Lifecycle Status from Knowledge Quality
s: Track governance lifecycle (`status`) and knowledge quality (`quality`) as two separate fields, reconcile the spec's Draft/Proposed ambiguity with two initial states, and treat the spec's `approval_status` as derived from `status`.
x: Separate Lifecycle Status from Knowledge Quality Context The spec defines a governance lifecycle (§13: Proposed … Retired), a quality status (§17: Draft … Superseded), and an approval status field (§16). The §13 transition example starts at "Draft → Review" while the lifecycle list starts at "Proposed". Problem How to represent these without redundant, contradictory fields? Options 1. One combined status field. 2. Two fields: status (governance lifecycle) and quality (content trust); approval status derived. 3. Three fields as listed in the spec. Evaluation Criteria Non-redundancy, expressiveness, validator enforceability, fidelity to spec. Trade-offs - Option 1 loses information (a published object can still be of limited quality). - Option 3 creates contradictions ( status: draft with approval status: approved ). Decision Proposed: option 2. - status : draft → proposed → under-review → validated → approved → published → (implemented) → deprecated → retired , plus rejected . Both draft and proposed are initial states; the LLM may set at most proposed . - quality : draft reviewed validated authoritative deprecated superseded , with constraints on the compatible status . - approval status is not stored ; it is derived ( approved: true for approved/published/implemented/deprecated in 00-system/governance/lifecycle.yaml ). Flagged deviation from spec §16 (which lists approval status as a field) — requires human approval. Consequences - Validator enforces status–quality compatibi

t: Store Typed Relationships as Front-Matter Keys
s: Represent typed relationships as top-level front-matter keys named after controlled relationship types, each holding a list of wikilinks; store each edge once and derive inverses on export.
x: Store Typed Relationships as Front-Matter Keys Context Relationships must be explicit and typed (spec §6), machine-readable, validated, and visible in Obsidian's graph. Problem Where and how to store typed relationships? Options 1. Top-level keys per relationship type: realized-by: ["X"] . 2. A nested list: relationships: [{type: realized-by, target: "X"}] . 3. Inline in body text with a convention (e.g. realized-by:: X ). Evaluation Criteria Obsidian graph visibility, validation simplicity, readability, portability. Trade-offs - Option 1: links in list properties are shown in Obsidian's graph and properties panel; simple to validate; relationship names share the key namespace with metadata fields (validator rejects unknown keys). - Option 2: cleaner namespace, but nested links are not reliably shown in Obsidian's graph. - Option 3: depends on plugins (e.g. Dataview). Decision Proposed: option 1. Vocabulary in 00-system/relationships/relationship-types.yaml with declared inverses. Each edge is stored once on the source object; either direction of a pair may be authored. Consequences - Validator rejects keys that are neither schema fields nor relationship types. - Body wikilinks remain untyped navigation, not relationships. Assumptions - Obsidian version with property (front-matter) link support. To verify per installed version. Constraints - Relationship names must be YAML-key safe (kebab-case). Related Architecture - Use Title-Based File Names for Knowledge Objects

t: Use Markdown and Git as the Initial Knowledge Store
s: Implement the knowledge graph initially as Markdown files with YAML front matter in a Git repository, navigable in Obsidian, validated by a script.
x: Use Markdown and Git as the Initial Knowledge Store Context The knowledge base must be personally usable now, governed, and transformable later into another knowledge-store technology (spec §19, §38). Problem Which storage and change-management mechanism to use for version 0.1? Options 1. Markdown + YAML front matter + Git (+ Obsidian as viewer). 2. A graph database (property graph or RDF triple store) from the start. 3. A wiki or document-management system. Evaluation Criteria Human readability, machine readability, change governance, tooling cost, portability, graph navigation. Trade-offs Option Gains Losses --- --- --- Markdown + Git readable, diffable, PR-based governance, free, portable no query language, validation must be built Graph database queries, constraints lower readability, no PR review, lock-in early Wiki easy editing weak structure and validation Decision Proposed: option 1. Typed relationships live in front matter so the files can be exported to a graph ( dakb.py export produces JSON, CSV and RDF Turtle). Consequences - Validation is implemented as a script and CI workflow. - Query capability is limited until export targets are used. Assumptions - Repository stays below a few thousand objects for the Markdown phase. Constraints - Must open in Obsidian (spec §38). Related Architecture - Store Typed Relationships as Front-Matter Keys - Use Title-Based File Names for Knowledge Objects

t: Use Title-Based File Names for Knowledge Objects
s: Name each knowledge object file after its title (unique across the repository) and keep the immutable ID in front matter, so Obsidian wikilinks and graph labels are human-readable.
x: Use Title-Based File Names for Knowledge Objects Context Obsidian resolves wikilinks by file name and labels graph nodes by file name. The spec example uses Information Architecture -style links. Problem Should files be named by ID ( DA-CON-0001.md ) or by title ( Data Architecture.md )? Options 1. Title-based file names, ID in front matter. 2. ID-based file names, title in front matter, links as Data Architecture . Evaluation Criteria Graph readability, link readability in plain text, rename stability, uniqueness. Trade-offs - Title-based: readable links and graph; renames require link updates (Obsidian does this automatically; outside Obsidian a script must). - ID-based: rename-stable; unreadable graph labels and raw links. Decision Proposed: option 1. The validator enforces title == file name , unique titles and unique IDs. IDs are immutable; titles may change via governed rename. Consequences - Titles may not contain / \ : ^ [ ] ; e.g. "ISO IEC 11179" instead of "ISO/IEC 11179" (the official form is kept as an alias). Assumptions - Exports use IDs as stable keys, so external stores are unaffected by renames. Constraints - File-system-safe characters only. Related Architecture - Use Markdown and Git as the Initial Knowledge Store

s: Five-level maturity model for an architecture knowledge base, from fragmented to executable, with observable indicators and automatable checks per level.
